You are writing copy for two audiences: (1) CFOs evaluating a software purchase and (2) end-user employees who will use the software daily.

The CFO version should emphasize _______, while the employee version should emphasize _______.

options.label: A
options.text: Ease of use; ROI and cost reduction

options.label: B
options.text: ROI and cost reduction; ease of use and daily workflow improvements

options.label: C
options.text: The company's origin story; technical specifications

explanation: CFOs make decisions based on financial outcomes (ROI, cost savings, time to value). End users care about how the tool affects their daily work (is it easy to learn, does it save them time, does it replace something painful). Same product, two completely different audience frames requiring different value propositions.

stem:
A startup founder pitches investors with the following: "Our product is the Uber of dog walking. We have no revenue yet, but our app has a really clean UI."

This pitch fails across multiple dimensions. Which combination of failures is most accurate?

options.label: B
options.text: Weak analogy (logic) + missing proof of traction (ethos) + wrong emphasis for the audience (voice)

explanation: The "Uber of X" analogy is weak because it tells investors nothing specific about the business model or market (logic failure). Having no revenue removes the strongest credibility signal investors look for (ethos failure). Leading with UI aesthetics instead of market size, unit economics, or growth rate misreads what investors need to hear (voice and audience frame failure).

stem:
A hospital sends the following text message to patients: "Per our records, your hemoglobin A1c remains elevated at 9.2%. Failure to achieve glycemic control may result in nephropathy, retinopathy, or peripheral neuropathy. Schedule follow-up immediately."

Rewrite this for a general patient audience. Which version best fixes the register and audience-frame problems while preserving accuracy?

options.label: A
options.text: "Your blood sugar levels are still too high. Over time, this can damage your kidneys, eyes, and nerves. Please call us to schedule a follow-up appointment."

options.label: B
options.text: "Hey! Your A1c is still kinda high. You should probably come in soon, lol."

options.label: C
options.text: "URGENT: You are at risk of organ failure. Call 911 immediately."

options.label: D
options.text: "Your hemoglobin A1c is 9.2%, which is above normal. Nephropathy is kidney disease. Retinopathy is eye disease. Neuropathy is nerve disease."

explanation: Option A translates the clinical language into plain English that a general audience can act on, while preserving medical accuracy. B is too casual for a health communication. C is alarmist and inaccurate. D just defines the jargon without changing the register or giving the patient a clear action step. This question tests the intersection of register (style), audience frame (voice), and clarity (grammar/diction).

stem:
You are ghostwriting a keynote speech for a Fortune 500 CEO addressing 3,000 employees after a difficult quarter. The CEO wants to acknowledge the struggle without sounding defeated, and rally the team without sounding out of touch.

Which combination of rhetorical and voice choices best fits this situation?

options.label: A
options.text: Open with industry statistics (logos), use formal academic register throughout, close with a policy announcement

options.label: B
options.text: Open with a personal admission of what kept the CEO up at night (ethos through vulnerability), move to specific data showing early signs of recovery (logos), close with anaphora ("We will...") to build collective momentum (pathos + rhetoric)

options.label: C
options.text: Open with a joke to lighten the mood, use casual slang throughout to seem relatable, close by blaming market conditions

options.label: D
options.text: Open with a quote from a celebrity, list every product the company makes, close with "any questions?"

explanation: This answer deploys Aristotle's triangle in sequence. The personal opening builds credibility and shows the CEO is not hiding behind corporate language. The recovery data provides rational hope without empty optimism. The anaphora at the close creates collective energy. This combination acknowledges reality (ethos), provides evidence for optimism (logos), and ends with emotional momentum (pathos) through a deliberate rhetorical device.
